must_have: For nausea due to dizziness or motion sickness, recommended drugs include antihistamines such as dimenhydrinate (Daramine, Drimite) and meclizine (Dramamine less drowsy).

answer:
## Bottom line
Yes — antiemetics such as [[F]]ondansetron[[/F]] and [[F]]trimethobenzamide[[/F]] are commonly used to control nausea/vomiting (including from acute gastroenteritis, chemotherapy, radiation, or surgery) so that oral intake and fluids can be better tolerated [1][2][3][12][13]; however, the retrieved findings pair antiemetic use with oral rehydration solution (ORS) as the actual mechanism for fluid replacement, and note ORS/hospital referral is used specifically when vomiting prevents fluids from staying down [4][5][11].

## Efficacy
- **Ondansetron**: one of the most commonly used antiemetics; "effective against nausea and vomiting of various etiologies" [1], works in the stomach to block signals to the brain causing nausea/vomiting [2], and is used to prevent nausea/vomiting from chemotherapy or radiation [12] and after surgery [13]. It is [[K]]not effective for motion sickness-related nausea[[/K]], underscoring that antiemetic choice should match the cause of nausea [8].
- **Trimethobenzamide**: approved specifically for postoperative nausea/vomiting and for nausea associated with gastroenteritis [3] — directly relevant to nausea that interferes with tolerating fluids/oral intake.
- **Olanzapine, palonosetron, granisetron**: described as possibly helping prevent/lessen chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting [9][10] — this evidence is scoped to chemotherapy, not fluid-intolerance from gastroenteritis or other causes.
- **Fluid management**: in a pediatric acute gastroenteritis (AGE) protocol, [[F]]ORS is the first-line strategy for significant vomiting, with hospital referral if ORS is not tolerated[[/F]] [4][11]. Separately, ORS (specifically hypotonic formulations, ≤250 mOsm/L) is described as the preferred method for mild-to-moderate dehydration from vomiting/diarrhea in AGE and is reported to **reduce the number of vomiting episodes** and the need for IV rehydration, without significantly increasing hyponatremia risk versus standard ORS [5].

## Safety & adverse effects
- **Ondansetron** — common adverse reactions (FDA labeling): headache, malaise/fatigue, constipation, diarrhea (for chemotherapy-induced nausea prevention); headache, constipation, diarrhea (for radiation-induced nausea prevention) [6]. Labeled warnings include QT prolongation, serotonin syndrome, myocardial ischemia, and masking of progressive ileus/gastric distension [7] — [[K]]relevant considerations before use[[/K]].
- No adverse-effect data were retrieved for trimethobenzamide, olanzapine, palonosetron, or granisetron in these findings.

## Population
- Ondansetron findings span nausea/vomiting from gastroenteritis, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and post-surgical settings [1][2][12][13], but it is specifically **not** shown effective for motion-sickness-related nausea [8].
- Trimethobenzamide's approved population is adults with postoperative nausea/vomiting or gastroenteritis-associated nausea [3].
- The ORS/vomiting-management protocol findings are from a [[K]]pediatric acute gastroenteritis study[[/K]] [4][5][11].
- Olanzapine/palonosetron/granisetron findings apply to patients undergoing chemotherapy [9][10].

## Evidence quality
- Findings [1]–[3], [6]–[8], [12]–[13] on ondansetron/trimethobenzamide draw on FDA drug labeling and general drug-information/web sources describing indications and labeled warnings — [[R]]this is regulatory/label-level evidence describing approved use and reported adverse effects, not a specific randomized efficacy trial result[[/R]].
- Findings [4], [9], [10], [11] are from **clinicaltrials.gov protocol descriptions**, which are [[R]]design intent (what a study is set up to test), not completed efficacy results[[/R]].
- Finding [5] references a numbered citation within a review-style statement (europepmc) characterizing ORS as the preferred rehydration method with specific reported effects on vomiting frequency — this is the most outcome-specific figure in the evidence set but its underlying study design/tier is not stated in the finding itself.

## Not addressed
The findings do not report head-to-head comparative efficacy figures (e.g., % reduction in vomiting, time to fluid tolerance) between different antiemetics, nor completed trial results confirming that any antiemetic directly increases the fraction of patients able to keep oral fluids down.

answer:
## Bottom line
For an insect bite/sting, low-potency topical corticosteroids (e.g., OTC hydrocortisone) are an accepted option for symptom relief [1][16], but general dermatology guidance advises [[K]]avoiding potent corticosteroids on the face[[/K]], with specialist exceptions only [5], and a specific high-potency product (augmented betamethasone dipropionate) explicitly instructs to [[F]]avoid use on the face[[/F]] [6].

## Efficacy
- Topical corticosteroids are indicated for inflammatory skin conditions "other than those arising from an infection," specifically including insect stings/bites, eczema, and contact dermatitis [1], and are used to relieve redness, itching, and swelling [16].
- For eczema/dermatitis-type presentations more broadly, first-line guidance is a **low-to-moderate potency topical corticosteroid ointment applied twice daily for two weeks or until symptoms resolve**, with potency increased if required [7][10][11]. This is not specifically a bite-treatment protocol in the findings.
- [[R]]Notably, a NICE evidence review found **no direct evidence** for self-care treatments including topical corticosteroids specifically for insect bites/stings[[/R]], and recommends pharmacist consultation instead of asserting efficacy [8].

## Safety & adverse effects
| Product/potency | Facial use guidance | Application | Other cautions |
|---|---|---|---|
| OTC hydrocortisone 1% (anti-itch, low potency) | Label doesn't prohibit facial use, but warns "For external use only. Do not get in eyes" [4] | 3–4 times daily (adults/children ≥12) [3] | Allergy alert: severe allergic reaction to bites/stings may require emergency care [2][18] |
| Betamethasone dipropionate (augmented, high potency) | [[F]]"Avoid use on the face, groin, or axillae"[[/F]] [6] | Once or twice daily; discontinue when controlled [12] | Not to be used with occlusive dressings unless physician-directed [13] |

- General guidance: potent corticosteroids should generally be avoided on the face and skin flexures; specialists occasionally prescribe them there in select circumstances [5].
- Corticosteroids suppress inflammation but are **not curative**; on stopping, a withdrawal/rebound flare can occur, rarely with redness extending beyond the treated area and burning/stinging worse than the original condition [9][17].
- Intralesional corticosteroid injections (a different route, using agents like triamcinolone acetonide [14]) should be avoided in atrophic skin or small lesions due to risk of tissue damage/ulceration [15] — relevant to steroid use on thin facial skin generally, though not specific to bites.

## Population
Findings apply to general users of topical corticosteroids for inflammatory skin conditions including insect bites/stings [1][16]; the OTC hydrocortisone label specifies adults and children 12 and over for the stated dosing [3]. No findings are specific to facial bites as a distinct population, nor to pediatric (<12) facial use.

## Evidence quality
The strongest-ranking evidence here is the **NICE evidence review**, which explicitly found no direct evidence for topical corticosteroids in treating insect bites/stings and instead recommends pharmacist advice [8] — this outranks product labels and general dermatology statements on the specific question of efficacy for bites. Product labeling (OTC hydrocortisone [2][3][4]; openFDA betamethasone dipropionate [6][12][13]) is regulatory/labeling-level guidance on use and warnings, not comparative efficacy data. General dermatology guidance on facial steroid avoidance [5] and eczema-treatment protocol [7][10][11] are guidance-level statements not derived from insect-bite-specific trials in these findings.

## Not addressed
The findings do not directly establish efficacy of topical corticosteroids for insect bites on the face specifically, nor do they identify a facial-safe potency tier or bite-specific dosing/duration for facial skin.

answer:
## Bottom line
Yes — testicular pain [[F]]can be a symptom of chlamydia[[/F]], most often because the infection spreads to the epididymis and causes epididymitis, which presents as unilateral testicular pain and swelling [1][5]. [[K]]This is typically seen in sexually active men, especially those under 35[[/K]] [2][3][10].

## Efficacy / Clinical presentation
- Chlamydial epididymitis presents as **unilateral, posterior testicular pain and swelling**, often with urethritis symptoms [1].
- Chlamydia and gonorrhea are the **most common infectious causes of epididymitis** in sexually active adults aged 18–35 [2][10][3].
- Chlamydia infection can **progress from urethritis to epididymitis** [4].
- Patient-facing guidance lists "**pain and swelling in one or both testicles**" directly as a symptom in men, and notes untreated infection can cause pain/swelling in the sperm-carrying tubes from the testicles [5][6].
- Epididymitis overall is a common cause of scrotal pain, with [[F]]over 500,000 new cases annually in North America[[/F]] [8]; in up to **35% of orchiepididymitis cases** the cause is a sexually transmitted organism such as C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae [9].
- Serologic studies found C. trachomatis IgG titers ≥64 in **75% of epididymitis patients vs. 40% of controls** (p<0.01), and IgA antibodies (titer ≥8) in **46% vs. 10%** (p<0.001) — supporting a chlamydial association with epididymitis cases [11][12].

## Safety / disease context
- Chlamydia is often **asymptomatic**, so testicular pain will not appear in every infected person, and absence of symptoms does not exclude infection [13].
- Broader disease spectrum includes cervicitis, urethritis, pelvic inflammatory disease, epididymitis, proctitis, neonatal conjunctivitis, and trachoma [7].
- If untreated in pregnancy, chlamydia can be transmitted to a baby during childbirth, causing pneumonia and eye problems — a distinct, non-testicular complication [14].

## Population
Findings apply mainly to **sexually active men aged 18–35** [2][3][10], the demographic in which chlamydia/gonorrhea are the leading infectious causes of epididymitis. General chlamydia symptom information (patient materials) applies to men broadly [5][6]. Findings on IgG/IgA serology come from epididymitis patients vs. controls without further age/subgroup breakdown [11][12].

## Evidence quality
- Clinical descriptions of chlamydial epididymitis and its epidemiology come from clinical review/case-context sources (europepmc) [1][2][3][8][9][10] — [[R]]observational/descriptive clinical literature, not randomized trials, but consistent across multiple sources[[/R]].
- The serologic case-control comparison (IgG/IgA titers in epididymitis patients vs. controls) is an **observational association study** with statistically significant differences reported [11][12] — this shows association, not that chlamydia definitively caused each case.
- Patient-education material (CDC-type web sources) corroborates the symptom list and general disease facts but is not primary research [5][6][13][14][15].
- No systematic review, guideline, or randomized trial is cited in these findings; conclusions rest on concordant descriptive/observational sources.

## Not addressed
The findings do not report the **frequency/percentage of chlamydia-infected men who develop testicular pain specifically**, nor treatment outcomes or resolution rates for chlamydial epididymitis.

## Bottom line
The evidence does not establish or endorse any single "best" brand of omeprazole [1]. Multiple manufacturers/retailers market FDA-listed omeprazole (or its enantiomer esomeprazole), including CVS Pharmacy, Kroger Company, A-S Medication Solutions, Somerset Therapeutics, Walmart's Equate line, and Amazon's Basic Care [1][2], and these are marketed as [[K]]generic/OTC equivalents to the brand-name product[[/K]] [3][4][5].

## Efficacy
- Walmart's Equate omeprazole magnesium capsule is approved via an [[F]]Abbreviated New Drug Application (ANDA)[[/F]], the regulatory pathway for a generic shown equivalent to a reference product, and matches the reference at 20 mg (equivalent to 20.6 mg omeprazole magnesium) [3][4].
- Amazon's Basic Care tablet is explicitly marketed as "Compare to Prilosec OTC®," also at 20 mg [5].
- However, a [[F]]randomized, open-label, crossover pharmacodynamic study[[/F]] in seven CYP2C19 extensive-metabolizer subjects found that acid-suppressive effects (24-h intragastric pH, % time pH>4) differed between original omeprazole and some generic brands, with [[R]]significantly greater inter-subject variability for Omeprazole-Towa and Ovulanze[[/R]] versus the original (Omeprazon) [6][17][16].
- All formulations (original and three generics) significantly raised 24-h intragastric pH versus placebo [7][18], but during the night-time period (20:00–08:00 h), [[K]]Omeprazole-Towa and Omerap were not significantly better than placebo[[/K]] [7][14].
- An international consensus paper notes omeprazole was the first PPI approved for OTC use, available at a standardized 20 mg OTC dose for 14-day courses — without endorsing a specific brand [8].

## Safety & adverse effects
- Most common adverse reactions in adults (incidence ≥2%): headache, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, and flatulence [10].
- In pediatric patients (1–16 years), the safety profile is similar to adults, except respiratory system events and fever were the most frequently reported reactions in pediatric studies [11].
- The cited pharmacodynamic study did not report brand-specific adverse-event differences — only differences in acid-suppression variability, which the authors state [[R]]"might be reflected in clinical outcomes"[[/R]] [15][6].

## Population
- Omeprazole delayed-release capsules are indicated for symptomatic GERD in patients ≥2 years of age [12].
- In combination with clarithromycin and amoxicillin, indicated for H. pylori eradication with duodenal ulcer disease (active or up to 1-year history) in adults [13].
- The generic-vs-original comparison study was conducted in a small sample of [[K]]seven healthy, H. pylori-negative CYP2C19 extensive metabolizers[[/K]], not in patients with active GERD, ulcer disease, or H. pylori infection [16].

## Evidence quality
- The brand-availability findings (CVS, Kroger, Equate, Basic Care) come from FDA/openfda drug labeling and product listings, which document [[R]]regulatory marketing status (e.g., ANDA) rather than comparative efficacy[[/R]] [1][2][3][4][5].
- The generic-vs-original acid-suppression comparison is a single small [[F]]prospective, randomized, open-label crossover study (n=7)[[/F]] — hypothesis-generating pharmacodynamic data, not a large or blinded efficacy/outcomes trial [17][16][6].
- The consensus/position paper on OTC PPI use provides expert-level context on omeprazole's regulatory history and dosing but does not compare brands [8].
- A ClinicalTrials.gov entry lists omeprazole as a studied intervention, which is protocol-level information only, not efficacy or brand data [9].

## Not addressed
The findings do not compare specific commercial brands (e.g., Prilosec vs. CVS vs. Kroger vs. Equate vs. Basic Care) head-to-head for efficacy or safety, and do not identify which named brand tested in the pharmacodynamic study (Omeprazon, Omeprazole-Towa, Ovulanze, Omerap) corresponds to any U.S. retail brand — so no brand-specific recommendation can be drawn from this evidence.

question: Whats a cluster headache?

must_have: Cluster headache is a type of chronic, severe, non-life-threatening headache.
Symptoms of cluster headache on the affected side may include tearing.
Cluster headache is usually one-sided, occurring in or around the eye.
Symptoms of cluster headache on the affected side may include a stuffy or runny nose.
Symptoms of cluster headache on the affected side may include a drooping eyelid.
Symptoms of cluster headache on the affected side may include redness of the eye.
There are effective treatments that can make cluster headache attacks less frequent.
There are effective treatments that can make cluster headache attacks less severe.
There are effective treatments that can make cluster headache attacks shorter.
Symptoms of cluster headache on the affected side may include sweating.
Cluster headache is characterized by bouts of frequent attacks of pain that can last from weeks to months.
A period of remission usually follows a bout of cluster headache.

answer:
## Bottom line
Cluster headache is [[K]]an uncommon, severe primary headache disorder[[/K]] causing [[F]]intense, one-sided pain in or around the eye, often described as one of the most painful conditions known[[/F]] [1], accompanied by ipsilateral autonomic features such as tearing, nasal congestion, eyelid swelling, and ptosis [2][15].

## Clinical features
- **Pain**: sudden, intense, fixed unilateral orbital, supraorbital, or temporal pain [2][4].
- **Associated autonomic symptoms**: conjunctival injection/tearing, nasal congestion/rhinorrhea, eyelid edema, facial sweating, miosis/ptosis, and restlessness or agitation [2][15].
- **Behavior during attacks**: patients are typically [[K]]agitated and pace restlessly[[/K]], in contrast to migraine patients who prefer to lie still in a dark room — restlessness can be severe enough to include head-banging [8].
- **Attack duration/frequency**: attacks last [[F]]15 minutes to 3 hours[[/F]] and occur [[F]]up to eight times a day, daily or almost daily, for weeks or months[[/F]] [3][4][11].
- **Diagnostic criteria (ICHD)**: at least five attacks of severe/very severe unilateral orbital, supraorbital, and/or temporal pain lasting 15 minutes to 3 hours untreated, with ipsilateral autonomic features [4].

## Subtypes
| Subtype | Pattern |
|---|---|
| Episodic (more common) | Attacks occur in "cluster periods" lasting weeks to months, with remission periods of **at least 1 month** [6], or specified elsewhere as **at least 3 months** between cluster periods [16] |
| Chronic (less common) | Lacks the extended remission seen in episodic disease; a "reasonable proportion" of patients have this form, marked by short or absent remission periods [5][14] |

## Severity and rarity
Cluster headache attacks are considered [[F]]the most serious among primary headaches[[/F]] due to their intensity, associated autonomic symptoms, and high daily frequency [13]. It is much rarer than migraine — affecting about [[F]]0.1% of the population[[/F]] versus roughly 14% for migraine [7][12].

## Diagnosis
Diagnosis is **clinical**, based on history; signs (red/watering eye, blocked/running nostril, ptosis ipsilateral to the pain) may be observed if the patient is seen during an attack [9].

## Treatment (as reported)
- **Acute**: parenteral triptans, dihydroergotamine, or oxygen [10].
- **Prevention**: verapamil, lithium, topiramate, divalproex, or galcanezumab (a monoclonal antibody), alone or in combination [10].

## Evidence quality
The findings draw on web/clinical reference summaries and a europepmc-sourced review-type source describing ICHD diagnostic criteria and clinical features [2][4][9][13][14], plus a clinicaltrials.gov-derived prevalence figure [7][12], which is protocol/registry-level context rather than efficacy trial data. No randomized trial results for treatment efficacy are included among the findings — treatment options are listed as recommended agents [10], not as outcomes data.

## Not addressed
The findings do not include efficacy figures (e.g., response rates, trial results) for the listed acute or preventive treatments, nor detailed epidemiology beyond the 0.1% prevalence estimate.

answer:
## Bottom line
Nausea and vomiting are among the most commonly reported adverse reactions to cephalexin (Keflex) [1][2][8], and although the drug can generally be taken with or without food [4][5][6], guidance specifically recommends taking it **with food if it upsets your stomach** [4]. The findings do not specifically address whether a "very low food intake" state increases the risk of vomiting.

## Efficacy
Not addressed by these findings — no data here on infection cure rates or clinical outcomes; the findings concern side effects and dosing/administration only [1][2][4][5][6].

## Safety & adverse effects
- [[F]]Nausea and vomiting are among the most common adverse reactions associated with cephalexin[[/F]], along with diarrhea, dyspepsia, and abdominal pain [1].
- In clinical trials, "nausea and vomiting, dyspepsia, gastritis, and abdominal pain have also occurred" [2].
- Minor gastrointestinal complaints reported during treatment include "abdominal discomfort, vomiting, diarrhea, loose bowel movements or nausea" [8].
- Patient-facing guidance (MedlinePlus) lists "nausea, vomiting, diarrhea" as effects to report to a doctor if severe or persistent [3].
- [[K]]Cephalexin is acid stable and "may be given without regard to meals," being rapidly absorbed after oral administration[[/K]] [6]; MedlinePlus similarly states it can be taken "with or without food" [5].
- [[F]]Cleveland Clinic guidance specifically advises: "You can take it with or without food. If it upsets your stomach, take it with food."[[/F]] [4]
- Cephalexin is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to cephalexin or other cephalosporins [7].

## Population
These findings apply generally to patients prescribed cephalexin for bacterial infections in various body sites [9], with the drug working by killing or inhibiting bacterial growth [11] and not being effective against viral infections such as colds or flu [12]. No findings distinguish outcomes for patients who have had low food intake or are otherwise nutritionally depleted [1]–[8].

## Evidence quality
[[R]]The GI adverse-effect findings come from the FDA drug label (openfda) and clinical trial adverse-reaction reporting [1][2][8], which is a standard, authoritative source for labeled side effects, though it reports aggregate trial-level frequencies rather than individualized risk factors like food intake.[[/R]] Administration guidance is drawn from the drug label's clinical pharmacology section [6] and patient-education sources (Cleveland Clinic, MedlinePlus) [4][5], which are practical dosing guidance rather than controlled-trial results on GI tolerability by food status.

## Not addressed
The findings do not address whether a "very low food intake" state specifically increases the likelihood of vomiting with cephalexin — no finding studies GI tolerability stratified by nutritional or food-intake status.

must_have: Valacyclovir (Valtrex) and acyclovir (Zovirax, Sitavig) are both antiviral drugs prescribed to treat infections caused by herpes simplex virus and varicella zoster virus.
Valacyclovir (Valtrex) and acyclovir (Zovirax, Sitavig) are used to treat cold sores, genital herpes, chicken pox and shingles.

answer:
## Bottom line
Valtrex (valacyclovir) is a prodrug that the body converts to acyclovir [1]; the key difference is [[F]]pharmacokinetic, not mechanistic[[/F]] — valacyclovir achieves ~3–5 fold greater oral bioavailability (~54–55%) than acyclovir (~15–20%) [3][4][24], which allows less frequent dosing for equivalent drug exposure [5]. Both are ultimately the same active moiety, acyclovir triphosphate, inhibiting viral DNA polymerase [2], and for most studied outcomes (genital herpes healing, zoster lesion resolution) they perform comparably [10][26], though valacyclovir showed a pain-duration advantage in zoster [11].

## Efficacy

| Attribute | Valacyclovir (Valtrex) | Acyclovir |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Prodrug converted to acyclovir in vivo [1] | Nucleoside analog phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase → inhibits viral DNA polymerase [2] |
| Oral bioavailability | ~54–55% [3][4][21], three- to five-fold that of acyclovir [3][4] | ~20% orally [24] |
| Genital herpes suppression dose | 500 mg once or twice daily (or 1 g once daily) [6] | 400 mg twice daily for up to 12 months [7] |
| Initial genital herpes treatment | — | 200 mg every 4 hours, 5×/day for 10 days [19] |
| Herpes zoster treatment | 1 g three times daily for 7 days [8] | 800 mg every 4 hours, 5×/day for 7–10 days [9] |
| First-episode genital herpes efficacy | No significant difference vs acyclovir in viral shedding duration (HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.84–1.18), time to healing (HR 1.08, 95% CI 0.92–1.27), pain duration (HR 1.0, 95% CI 0.85–1.18), symptom resolution (HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.85–1.22) [10] | Same trial comparator [10] |
| Zoster lesion resolution | Equally effective as acyclovir [11][26] | Equally effective as valacyclovir [11][26] |
| Zoster-associated pain duration | Significantly more effective than acyclovir in a large comparative study (patients ≥50 years) [11] | Less effective for this endpoint in same study [11] |
| Postherpetic neuralgia pain | At least as effective as acyclovir [25] | Comparator [25] |
| Suppressive effect (guideline view) | Greater bioavailability, but improved *suppressive clinical effect* over acyclovir not demonstrated [16][20] | Comparator [16][20] |

Dosing at valacyclovir 250 mg four times daily produces essentially the same acyclovir AUC as acyclovir 800 mg five times daily [5]; valacyclovir 1000 mg three times daily produces a similar acyclovir AUC to IV acyclovir 5 mg/kg every 8 hours [22] — illustrating that valacyclovir's oral dosing approximates IV acyclovir exposure [12][22].

## Safety & adverse effects
- Valacyclovir tablets carry labeled warnings for **thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura/hemolytic uremic syndrome, acute renal failure, CNS effects, and severe cutaneous adverse reactions**; most common adverse reactions (>10% in ≥1 indication) are headache, nausea, and abdominal pain [13].
- In head-to-head first-episode genital herpes treatment, adverse events were comparable between valacyclovir and acyclovir [10].
- IV acyclovir generates higher peak plasma levels than oral valacyclovir [23]; higher acyclovir peaks may increase risk of **kidney toxicity from crystal precipitation in renal tubules** [12]. Valacyclovir safety at doses above FDA-approved levels — particularly in immunocompromised patients — remains controversial [12].
- Both drugs are renally eliminated and require dose adjustment in renal impairment; acyclovir dosing is specifically modified below creatinine clearance 30 mL/min/1.73 m² [14].

## Population
Findings cover [[K]]immunocompetent and HIV-1–infected adults with genital herpes, herpes zoster, and cold sores (herpes labialis), plus pediatric cold sores and chickenpox for valacyclovir[[/K]] [6][15][17]. The large zoster comparative study specifically included patients ≥50 years of age [11]. Valacyclovir's labeled indications (cold sores, genital herpes treatment/suppression/transmission reduction, zoster in adults; cold sores and chickenpox in children) are broader than the acyclovir indications captured here [15]. Valacyclovir may be taken without regard to meals [18].

## Evidence quality
Evidence includes labeled FDA dosing information (openfda) [6][7][8][9][13][15][17][19], a guideline-level synthesis noting no demonstrated suppressive-effect advantage for valacyclovir [16][20], pharmacokinetic study data on bioavailability [4], and a randomized head-to-head trial in first-episode genital herpes reporting hazard ratios with 95% CIs [10], plus a review citing a "large comparative study" in zoster [11][26]. [[R]]The randomized trial [10] and the large comparative zoster study [11] rank above pharmacokinetic/PK-modeling findings and drug-label dosing tables as direct efficacy evidence, though FDA labeling remains authoritative for dosing[[/R]]. No systematic review or formal guideline-graded recommendation ranking the two drugs was retrieved beyond the noted guideline statement on suppression [16][20].

## Not addressed
The findings do not report comparative cost, formulation availability, or head-to-head efficacy/safety data outside genital herpes and zoster (e.g., cold sores, chickenpox, or immunocompromised populations specifically).

answer:
## Bottom line
Vestibular neuritis (now preferably termed acute unilateral vestibulopathy, also called vestibular neuronitis) is an [[F]]inflammatory disorder of the vestibular portion of the eighth cranial nerve[[/F]], generally viral or postviral in origin [1][2], causing [[F]]acute, spontaneous, peripheral vestibular dysfunction[[/F]] with rapid-onset severe vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and gait instability [1][3], and [[K]]without hearing loss or tinnitus[[/K]] (distinguishing it from labyrinthitis) [5][16].

## Efficacy
Not applicable in the treatment-efficacy sense — the findings describe the disease and its management rather than a controlled efficacy comparison. Management is [[F]]supportive[[/F]], consisting of antiemetics, antihistamines, and benzodiazepines, with vestibular rehabilitation begun once acute nausea/vomiting are controlled [11][23]. The condition is [[F]]self-limited[[/F]]: symptoms such as nystagmus, vertigo, and nausea typically reduce within 14 days via spontaneous central rebalancing of vestibular tone [17][18], though full resolution of all vestibular symptoms can take [[F]]weeks to months[[/F]] [8][22].

## Safety & adverse effects
No drug-specific adverse-effect data are reported in these findings; rather, the "risk" content concerns diagnostic/clinical features that must be distinguished from more serious central causes.
- [[K]]Must be differentiated from central causes such as cerebrovascular syndromes (stroke)[[/K]], which can mimic the same history/exam findings — a clinical diagnosis challenge, not a treatment risk [8].
- Cardinal signs: acute rotatory vertigo, Romberg's sign with falls toward the affected ear, horizontal-torsional spontaneous nystagmus beating toward the *unaffected* ear, nausea, and ipsilateral hyporesponsiveness on caloric testing [7][15].
- No cochlear symptoms (no hearing loss, no tinnitus) — a feature used to rule out labyrinthitis or other cochlear pathology [5][16].

## Population
Affects patients presenting to dizziness clinics, accounting for [[F]]3.2%–9% of consultations[[/F]] in specialized dizziness clinics, with an [[F]]incidence of 3.5 cases per 100,000 individuals[[/F]] [10][13]; mean age at onset ranges [[K]]10 to 50 years[[/K]] per one source [10]. It is the [[F]]third most common peripheral vestibular disorder[[/F]] after benign paroxysmal positional vertigo and Ménière disease [4][20]. Proposed/associated causes include viral infection or postviral inflammation [2], possible HSV-1 reactivation in vestibular ganglia (evidence "circumstantial") [9], ischemia of the anterior vestibular artery [4], and COVID-19 as a reported novel etiological factor in case reports/cohort studies [12].

## Evidence quality
The findings derive from narrative/clinical review sources ("web") and an europepmc-sourced review, describing established clinical diagnostic criteria, epidemiology, and standard supportive management rather than randomized trial efficacy data. [[R]]No systematic review, guideline, or RCT results for a specific treatment are cited here — the evidentiary basis is descriptive/observational clinical characterization of the disease, not comparative-effectiveness evidence[[/R]] [1][4][8][10][13]. The viral-causation mechanism is explicitly flagged as resting on "circumstantial" evidence (postmortem HSV-1 detection) rather than confirmed causal proof [9].

## Not addressed
The findings do not cover comparative efficacy of specific treatments (e.g., corticosteroids, antiviral agents) for vestibular neuritis, nor randomized trial outcome data, prognosis stratifiers, or long-term recurrence rates.

question: What is a neurological issue

must_have: A neurological issue is a problem that affects the nervous system.
Neurological issues are conditions where abilities such as speaking, moving, thinking are impaired.
nice_to_have: Epilepsy is a neurological issue.
Stroke is a neurological issue.
Alzheimer's disease is a neurological issue.
Peripheral neuropathy is a neurological issue.
The nervous system is in charge of human abilities such as the ability to speak, move, think.
The nervous system includes the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves.
Multiple sclerosis is a neurological issue.

answer:
## Bottom line
A neurological issue (neurological disorder) is a condition that disrupts normal functioning of the nervous system — brain, spinal cord, and peripheral/autonomic nerves — via structural, biochemical, or electrical abnormalities [1][2][17], producing symptoms that affect [[K]]movement, sensation, cognition, and mood[[/K]] [3][6][21].

## What it affects
- **Anatomic scope:** central nervous system (brain, spinal cord) and peripheral nervous system, the latter dividing into the somatic (voluntary movement) and autonomic (involuntary activity) systems [5]; disorders span the brain, spinal cord, cranial and peripheral nerves, and autonomic nervous system [2].
- **Mechanism:** [[F]]cellular changes (loss of neurons, axonal injury, blood-brain barrier disruption) or molecular changes (altered membrane excitability, oxidative stress)[[/F]] [1]; more broadly, structural, biochemical, or electrical abnormalities [17].
- **Causes:** genetic, developmental, acquired, and degenerative etiologies [19].

## Symptoms
- **Sensory/consciousness:** loss of sensation, confusion, altered levels of consciousness, seizures, pain, memory loss [3][17].
- **Muscle/movement:** weakness, tremor, paralysis, involuntary movements (tics), gait abnormalities, clumsiness, spasms, rigidity/spasticity, slowed movements [7].
- **Cognitive:** aphasia, poor memory, apraxia, agnosia/prosopagnosia, poor concentration, acalculia, spatial difficulty, dementia, hemineglect [8].
- **Overall:** physical, cognitive, emotional, and behavioral symptoms (pain, confusion, mood changes, coordination difficulty) [21]; severity ranges from minor (a foot "falling asleep") to life-threatening (coma from brainstem stroke) [9].

## Categories / examples
- **Neurodegenerative:** Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, ALS, multiple sclerosis — progressive neuronal loss, protein misfolding, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation [11].
- **Neurotraumatic:** stroke, traumatic brain injury, spinal cord injury — pathogenesis involves ATP depletion, loss of ion homeostasis, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation [10].
- **Other disease groupings:** disorders of the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves; muscle and neuromuscular disorders; spinal cord injury [15]; dementia and cerebrovascular disease are cited as additional examples [16].
- **General examples:** Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis, meningitis, among hundreds of recognized disorders [4][20].
- **Clinical-trial usage:** trial protocols use "neurological disorder/issue" to mean history of CNS disease such as tumor, epilepsy, or stroke [13], and exclusion criteria list conditions such as Parkinson's disease, ALS, cerebrovascular stroke, and psychiatric disorders (major depression, generalized anxiety, mania) [12].

## Population / burden
The WHO estimates neurological disorders currently affect as many as [[F]]one billion people worldwide[[/F]], with numbers expected to increase, representing a major and growing public health challenge [14][18].

## Evidence quality
[[R]]Findings are drawn from general web/health-reference sources describing definitions, mechanisms, and symptom lists [1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8][9][17][19][20][21], a WHO burden estimate [14][18], and clinical-trial protocol language that reflects design-level (not efficacy) definitions of "neurological disorder" for eligibility/exclusion purposes [12][13][16].[[/R]] No systematic reviews, guidelines, or trial efficacy results are included; this is definitional/descriptive evidence, not treatment-outcome evidence.

## Not addressed
The findings do not cover diagnosis, treatment efficacy, or safety of interventions for specific neurological disorders — only what a neurological issue is, its mechanisms, symptoms, categories, and prevalence.

question: Is it safe to take zyrtec / Claritin while breastfeeding?

must_have: Second-generation antihistamines, such as Cetirizine (Zytrec) and Loratadine (Claritin), are considered the drug of choice for breastfeeding mothers compared to first-generation antihistamines.
Breastfeeding mothers taking Cetirizine (Zytrec) or Loratadine (Claritin) should monitor the infant for irritability, jitteriness, or drowsiness.
The recommendation for breastfeeding mothers taking Cetirizine (Zytrec) or Loratadine (Claritin) is to take the lowest effective dose.
Antihistamines pass on to breastmilk of women taking the drug.
If you are nursing, it is advisable to consult your healthcare provider before taking an antihistamine agent.
nice_to_have: Cetirizine (Zytrec) and Loratadine (Claritin) are used for treating allergic symptoms of the upper respiratory tract, the eye, and the skin.

answer:
## Bottom line
For **cetirizine (Zyrtec)**, the weight of pharmacologic and clinical-guideline evidence supports that [[F]]small occasional doses are acceptable during breastfeeding[[/F]] [1][22], with international guidelines and the LactMed database naming it a recommended/acceptable antihistamine choice if one is needed [1][21][24]. Explicit findings on **loratadine (Claritin)** are more limited, but several reviews identify it as a preferred antihistamine during lactation because it (like cetirizine) is excreted into milk in very low amounts [9][10][12]. Product labels for cetirizine, however, still advise caution or "ask your doctor" due to a lack of formal clinical studies [14][15][20][28].

## Efficacy
The evidence retrieved concerns milk transfer/infant exposure, not symptom-relief efficacy of cetirizine or loratadine themselves — no findings report allergy-symptom outcome data for lactating mothers. What is quantified is **infant drug exposure via milk**, used as a safety metric:

| Study | Measure | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Human lactation study [2] | Peak/average milk concentration; infant dose | Peak ~49 mcg/L at ~2h; average 21.1 mcg/L over 24h; infant dose 3.1 mcg/kg/day = **1.77%** of maternal weight-adjusted dose [2][27] |
| Validation study, 228 samples [3] | Milk concentration | Median **13 mcg/L** (range 0.65–65 mcg/L) [3] |
| PopPK model (35 women) [4] | Relative Infant Dose (RID) | Mean **1.99%**, highest at Cmax **3.36%** [4][17] |
| Related popPK analysis [5] | RID | Up to **3.53%** at highest [5] |
| WHO threshold [6] | Compatibility cutoff | RID <10% = compatible; cetirizine met this in **all tested scenarios** [6] |
| Systematic review of antihistamines [7] | RID range across 10 antihistamines | **0.3%** (terfenadine) to **4.5%** (clemastine); cetirizine included, all <5% [7] |

These figures are consistently well below the WHO 10% compatibility threshold [6], supporting compatibility rather than measuring clinical benefit.

## Safety & adverse effects
- **Infant exposure is low**: RID estimates for cetirizine range from ~1.77–3.53% [2][4][5][17][27], and cetirizine met WHO's <10% compatibility criterion in all scenarios modeled [6].
- **Possible infant effects with higher/prolonged dosing**: [[F]]larger doses or more prolonged maternal use may cause drowsiness or other effects in the infant, or decrease milk supply[[/F]], particularly with a sympathomimetic (e.g., pseudoephedrine) or before lactation is established [1][23].
- **Reported infant symptoms in a follow-up study**: mothers of antihistamine-exposed breastfed infants reported [[F]]irritability/colicky symptoms in about 10% of infants[[/F]], with drowsiness also reported [13].
- **First-generation antihistamines** (sedating types) should be avoided while breastfeeding due to sedative properties; loratadine, fexofenadine, and cetirizine are identified as preferred alternatives [12].
- **Labeling caution**: manufacturer/product labels state there are [[F]]no adequate studies in women to determine infant risk[[/F]] and advise weighing risks/benefits or consulting a doctor [14][15][20][28]; this reflects regulatory caution rather than a demonstrated harm signal, contrasted with guideline/database assessments [7][8][20].
- Ophthalmic (eye-drop) cetirizine use by the mother is noted to pose little risk to the breastfed infant [26], and cetirizine has been used successfully for persistent breast pain during breastfeeding [25] — narrow, specific use cases.

## Population
Findings apply to **breastfeeding women** taking oral cetirizine (10 mg once daily is the noted recommended adult dose [19]) and their **exclusively or partially breastfed infants** [2][27]. Data derive from human lactation pharmacokinetic studies (35 women [4]; 228 milk samples [3]) and reviews/guideline statements (LactMed, WHO Working Group, systematic reviews) [1][6][7][8]. Explicit named studies on **loratadine** in lactating populations are not detailed beyond general review statements grouping it with cetirizine as low-excretion/preferred [9][10][12]; no loratadine-specific RID or milk-concentration figures are given in the findings.

## Evidence quality
- [[R]]The strongest evidence for cetirizine is the WHO Working Group compatibility framework (RID <10%) applied to multiple human lactation studies and popPK models[[/R]] — this outranks individual case reports or label language because it aggregates quantitative human milk-transfer data [4][5][6][17].
- A systematic review of 10 antihistamines (RID 0.3–4.5%) provides comparative, evidence-hierarchy-appropriate context but simultaneously notes most product labels recommend avoidance due to "lack of evidence," reflecting a gap between regulatory labeling and clinical/PK evidence [7][8][20].
- LactMed (NIH database) and international guideline statements are authoritative synthesis sources for lactation safety and directly support cetirizine's acceptability [1][21][24].
- Manufacturer labels (cetirizine injectable, OTC generic) are the most conservative source, reflecting regulatory default caution rather than newly demonstrated risk [14][15][28].
- The infant-symptom follow-up report (irritability/colicky symptoms, drowsiness) is a lower-tier observational/telephone follow-up study, not a controlled trial [13].
- No systematic review, guideline, or PK study specific to loratadine with quantitative RID/milk-concentration data was retrieved; loratadine's favorable status rests on narrative review statements only [9][10][12].

## Not addressed
The findings do not report loratadine-specific relative infant dose, milk concentration, or infant-outcome data comparable to what exists for cetirizine [9][10][12]. They also do not address efficacy of either drug for maternal allergy symptom control, nor long-term (beyond initial exposure) infant developmental outcomes.

## Bottom line

## Efficacy
Not applicable — this question concerns transmissibility of a dermatologic reaction, not a treatment's effectiveness.

## Safety & adverse effects
- The rash itself and the blister fluid are **not contagious**: "The rash isn’t contagious. If someone has a rash, touching that rash won’t cause a rash on your skin" [2]; "The blister fluid itself is not contagious" [3].

## Bottom line
Acute bronchitis is [[K]]a self-limiting infection of the bronchial airways, distinct from pneumonia which infects the lung tissue itself[[/K]] [1][12]. It usually stays mild, but [[F]]pneumonia can occur as a complication of acute bronchitis, particularly in older people[[/F]] [2][3] — so bronchitis does not routinely "turn into" pneumonia, but it can be complicated by it in a specific subgroup.

## Efficacy
Not applicable — this question concerns disease course/complications, not a treatment's effectiveness. The findings do note that treating acute exacerbations of COPD (a related but distinct entity) with purulent sputum and increased shortness of breath reduces mortality by 77% and treatment failure by 53% [11], but this pertains to COPD exacerbations, not acute bronchitis progressing to pneumonia.

## Safety & adverse effects / disease course
- Acute bronchitis: inflammation of the bronchial airways, [[K]]typically viral, self-limiting, treated mainly symptomatically[[/K]] [1][7][9].
- Pneumonia: infection of the lung tissue where air sacs fill with microorganisms, fluid, and inflammatory cells, impairing lung function [12]; reported complications of pneumonia itself include pleural effusion/empyema, lung abscess, ARDS, sepsis, and disseminated infection [13].
- [[F]]Pneumonia may occur as a complication of acute bronchitis, particularly in older people[[/F]] [2][3] — this is the direct evidentiary link between the two conditions.
- Diagnostically, the two conditions sit on a spectrum: acute bronchitis is diagnosed only after pneumonia is ruled out, either clinically or radiographically [4][8]. Absence of tachycardia (>100 bpm), tachypnea (>24/min), fever (>38°C), or focal consolidation/egophony/fremitus lowers the likelihood a cough illness is actually pneumonia rather than bronchitis, obviating need for chest radiograph [6].

- The bronchitis–pneumonia complication link cited applies particularly to **older people** [2][3].
- Acute bronchitis as defined here affects adults and children **without underlying pulmonary disease** [7].
- Acute exacerbations of *chronic* bronchitis (a different entity, often in COPD) may be triggered by bacterial or viral infection [10], and antibiotic treatment in that COPD-exacerbation context reduces mortality and treatment failure [11] — this population/context is distinct from acute bronchitis in otherwise healthy people.
- Case-level imaging findings (bilateral pneumonia on chest radiograph [14]; parenchymal consolidation with nodules and lymphadenopathy on CT [15]; unremarkable bronchoscopy with negative AFB and MTB testing [16]) come from an individual case report and illustrate pneumonia's radiographic appearance rather than establishing a bronchitis-to-pneumonia pathway.

## Evidence quality
[[R]]The core claim — that pneumonia may complicate acute bronchitis, especially in older adults — rests on general clinical/guideline-style statements (BMJ Best Practice, NICE) rather than a controlled study designed to test progression risk[[/R]] [2][3]. Diagnostic-distinction guidance draws on ACCP evidence-based guidelines [4] and clinical decision criteria [6], which outrank a single case report. The imaging/bronchoscopy findings [14][15][16] derive from a case report, the lowest tier of evidence here, and should not be generalized. No randomized or systematic-review data specifically quantifying the rate of bronchitis progressing to pneumonia were retrieved.

## Not addressed
The findings do not report a specific incidence/rate at which acute bronchitis progresses to pneumonia, nor a mechanistic or longitudinal study establishing causation (only that pneumonia "may occur as a complication," without a quantified risk).

answer:
## Bottom line
No — across general medical descriptions of abscesses, pain is repeatedly described as a **defining, expected feature** [1][2][3][11][14], making a painless presentation atypical rather than common. Some abscess-*grading* schemes and a few distinct conditions can present without pain, but these describe lower-grade inflammation or different entities, not typical frank abscesses [5][6][8][9].

## Efficacy
Not applicable — this question concerns symptom presentation, not treatment efficacy.

## Safety & adverse effects / Clinical presentation
- **Cutaneous/subcutaneous abscesses:** [[F]]"Symptoms and signs are pain and a tender and firm or fluctuant swelling."[[/F]] [1]; more fully, "pain, heat, swelling, tenderness, and redness" [2][14].
- **General skin abscesses:** "They are red, raised, and painful" [3].
- **Deep abscesses (e.g., abdominal):** [[F]]"Most people with an abdominal abscess have constant abdominal pain and a fever."[[/F]] [4]; specifically, "local pain and tenderness and systemic symptoms, especially fever... are typical" [12], and "most people have constant discomfort or pain, feel generally sick (malaise), and often have a fever" [13].
- **General abscess symptoms:** "local pain, tenderness, warmth, and swelling (if abscesses are near the skin layer) or constitutional symptoms (if abscesses are deep)" [11]. Abscesses themselves are simply "collections of pus in confined tissue spaces, usually caused by bacterial infection" [10].
- **Exceptions/nuance:** [[K]]Certain breast abscess grading schemes classify lower grades of inflammation as occurring "without abscess symptoms/signs (i.e., fever, pain, drainage, fluctuation)"[[/K]] — either with minimal skin inflammation and no palpable mass [5], or with a palpable mass but still without pain/fever/drainage/fluctuation [6]. These describe milder inflammatory stages, not typical established abscesses.
- **Analogous conditions:** Painless presentation of a related suppurative/inflammatory condition (appendicitis) is explicitly called "very uncommon" and diagnostically challenging [7], supporting the general principle that painless inflammatory/infective presentations are recognized but rare.
- **Mimics/distinct entities:** Cystic lymphangiomas "typically present as painless masses," which helps distinguish them from (usually painful) abscesses [8]. Actinomycetoma/mycetoma "typically presents as painless, progressively enlarging subcutaneous lesions with fistulous tracts" — a different chronic granulomatous infection, not a typical abscess [9].

## Population
Findings cover cutaneous/subcutaneous abscesses [1][2][3][14], deep/abdominal abscesses [4][12][13], general abscess pathophysiology [10][11], breast abscess grading specifically [5][6], and unrelated/analogous conditions used for contrast (appendicitis [7], cystic lymphangioma [8], actinomycetoma [9]). No age- or comorbidity-specific subgroup data are given.

## Evidence quality
The core claims rest on general medical/web reference descriptions of abscess symptoms [1][2][3][4][10][11][12][13][14] — consensus descriptive statements rather than graded studies, but consistent across multiple independent sources. The exceptions come from a specific breast abscess grading classification [5][6] and case-level descriptions of analogous/mimicking conditions [7][8][9] — narrower, lower-tier evidence not generalizable to abscesses broadly.

## Not addressed
The findings do not provide incidence rates or proportions (e.g., "X% of abscesses are painless") for any abscess type, so the literal frequency of painless abscesses cannot be quantified from this evidence.

question: So prednisone is a cortisone type medication?

must_have: Prednisone is a synthetic drug that derives from cortisone.
nice_to_have: Corticosteroid medications are used to decrease inflammation and suppress the immune system in cases of overactivity.
Prednisone, Cortisone and Hydrocortisone are corticosteroid medications.

answer:
## Bottom line
Yes — prednisone is a [[F]]glucocorticoid[[/F]], the class of adrenocortical (corticosteroid) hormones that also includes cortisone itself [1][11]. It is not cortisone, but a **synthetic analog** structurally and functionally related to the naturally occurring glucocorticoids cortisone and hydrocortisone [2][5].

## Mechanism / classification
- Prednisone belongs to the glucocorticoid subclass of adrenocortical steroids, which occur both naturally and synthetically [1].
- [[K]]The two naturally occurring glucocorticoids are hydrocortisone and cortisone[[/K]]; prednisone is a synthetic analog of these, engineered for potent anti-inflammatory activity rather than for salt-retaining/replacement properties [2].
- Chemically it is a steroid (C21H26O5; 17,21-dihydroxypregna-1,4-diene-3,11,20-trione), reflecting its structural kinship to cortisone/hydrocortisone [5].
- Like other glucocorticoids, prednisone produces broad metabolic effects and modifies immune responses [3], and it acts via glucocorticoid receptors to promote anti-inflammatory proteins and inhibit pro-inflammatory proteins [8].

## Efficacy
- Prednisone's therapeutic use is as a potent anti-inflammatory agent across "disorders of many organ systems," in contrast to natural glucocorticoids, which are used for hormone replacement [2].
- In a specific clinical context, early RCTs found oral prednisone significantly reduced in-stent restenosis (ISR) rates in patients with an elevated inflammatory response (elevated CRP) after bare-metal stent (BMS) implantation [9]. A meta-analysis of three RCTs (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day, tapered over 40–45 days) found [[F]]no reduction in death but significantly reduced ISR (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.37–0.97, p=0.04) and target vessel revascularization (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.34–0.92, p=0.02) at 6 months post-PCI[[/F]] [10].

## Safety & adverse effects
- As a corticosteroid, prednisone carries the class-level risk of reversible hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis suppression, with potential corticosteroid insufficiency after treatment withdrawal, and increased infection risk [6].
- Initial dosing ranges from 5 mg to 60 mg/day depending on the disease being treated, reflecting the wide range of conditions and intensities for which it is prescribed [7].

## Population
- Findings on adrenocortical insufficiency indicate that natural glucocorticoids (hydrocortisone or cortisone) are the **first-choice** agents for that endocrine replacement indication, with synthetic analogs like prednisone used adjunctively (e.g., alongside mineralocorticoids) [4][12].
- The ISR/cardiac stent data apply specifically to coronary artery disease (CAD) patients with elevated CRP who received bare-metal stents [9][10] — this is a narrow population, not general anti-inflammatory use.

## Evidence quality
- Classification and mechanism statements [1][2][3][5][8][11] and safety-class labeling language [6][7] derive from drug-label/reference (web, openfda) sources describing prednisone generically as a corticosteroid — these are descriptive/labeling-level, not primary trial data.
- [[R]]The ISR findings rest on RCTs and a meta-analysis of three RCTs[[/R]], which outrank observational data, but are specific to the BMS/CAD/elevated-CRP context and to surrogate/procedural endpoints (ISR, revascularization) rather than general anti-inflammatory efficacy [9][10].

## Not addressed
The findings do not provide a direct clinical comparison of prednisone versus cortisone (e.g., relative potency, dosing equivalence, or interchangeable use) beyond noting prednisone is a synthetic analog of cortisone/hydrocortisone [2][5].

question: what is the difference between fissure vs hemorrhoids?

must_have: Anal fissures are tears in the anal tissue caused by trauma
Hemorrhoids are normal vascular structures that can grow abnormally due to various factors
Both anal fissures and hemorrhoids can cause bleeding and discomfort
Hemorrhoids can lead to rectal bleeding, irritation, and can prolapse
Hemorrhoids usually don't cause pain unless there is a strangulation or blood clot present
Anal fissures are accompanied by severe pain exacerbated by defecation
Diagnosis of anal fissures and hemorrhoids can usually be made through examination based on appearance

answer:
## Bottom line
An **anal fissure** is a linear tear in the anal canal lining that causes tearing pain triggered by defecation [1], whereas **hemorrhoids** are normal, swollen vascular cushions in the anal canal that are usually painless unless thrombosed or complicated, and instead cause bleeding, itching, discomfort, or prolapse [2][3][4]. Both are common, generally benign anorectal conditions that often respond to non-operative care [9].

## Efficacy
This question is about diagnosis/pathophysiology rather than a treatment efficacy comparison, but the findings do describe first-line management for each:

| Feature | Anal fissure | Hemorrhoids |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | Linear tear from dentate line toward anal verge [1] | Normal sinusoidal vascular cushions of the anal canal [2][14][19] |
| Typical cause | Trauma from constipation or diarrhea [1] | Vascular cushions becoming symptomatic (dilatation, thrombosis, strangulation in acute disease) [15] |
| Hallmark symptom | [[F]]Tearing pain triggered by defecation, lasting hours[[/F]], sometimes bright red blood on tissue [1][17] | [[F]]Painless unless thrombosed[[/F]]; bleeding, itching, discomfort, prolapse [3][20] |
| Classification | Acute (fresh, "paper-cut") vs chronic (>8 weeks, deeper tear ± fleshy growths) [6] | Grade I–IV by degree of prolapse [5]; also internal vs external by position relative to the dentate/pectinate line [2][8] |
| First-line treatment | Sitz baths, bulking agents (psyllium fiber) [10] | Increased fiber, avoiding straining; sitz baths advised though data limited [11] |
| Refractory treatment | Topical nitroglycerin (heals ~half of chronic fissures), calcium channel blockers, botulinum toxin, or lateral internal sphincterotomy [12][18] | Rubber band ligation, infrared coagulation; surgical hemorrhoidectomy required for grade 4 disease [13] |

[[K]]Location and innervation differ mechanistically[[/K]]: internal hemorrhoids lie above the dentate line with visceral innervation and are not painful (may bleed/prolapse), while external hemorrhoids lie below it with somatic innervation and can cause discomfort — a different pain mechanism from fissures [4].

## Safety & adverse effects
- Fissures: bright red blood on toilet tissue may accompany the tearing pain [1]. Atypical (lateral or multiple) fissures may signal underlying disease — Crohn's disease, HIV, hematologic malignancy, syphilis, or tuberculosis — versus the typical anterior midline location seen in 73% of cases [7].
- Hemorrhoids: acute hemorrhoidal disease ("hemorrhoidal crisis") involves persistent bleeding or acute anal pain from dilatation, thrombosis, or strangulation [15]; chronic disease has milder or subclinical symptoms between acute episodes [16]. Significant pain occurs only with thrombosis [3].
- Both conditions can, in some cases, require surgical management despite usually responding to conservative therapy [9].

## Population
The findings describe general adult anorectal disease presentations rather than a specific trial population. Fissure findings note that atypical presentations (lateral/multiple) warrant evaluation for systemic disease [7]. Hemorrhoid grading and treatment escalation (e.g., banding failures, grade 3–4 disease) point to a subgroup needing surgical consultation [13].

## Evidence quality
[[R]]The findings draw on narrative/clinical review sources and society best-practice statements (e.g., europepmc BPA-numbered guidance) rather than randomized trials — appropriate for descriptive pathophysiology and diagnostic distinction, but this is not comparative efficacy evidence[[/R]] [1][2][3][11][13]. No systematic review, RCT, or trial registry data comparing fissure vs. hemorrhoid treatments head-to-head is present in these findings.

## Not addressed
The findings do not provide a head-to-head trial or systematic review directly comparing fissures and hemorrhoids as a category; they instead describe each condition separately (definition, symptoms, classification, treatment) and let the contrast be drawn from those descriptions. No epidemiologic data on relative prevalence or coexistence of the two conditions is included.

question: What causes genital warts?

must_have: Condyloma acuminata, also known as anogenital warts, are manifestations of HPV infection that occur in the anogenital area.
nice_to_have: Warts are not required for transmission of HPV.
Human papillomavirus (HPV) is transmitted through contact with infected skin or mucosa.
Genital warts are usually not symptomatic apart from the visual appearance.
Warts are highly contagious.
Genital warts could be irritated in rare cases.
Genital warts are typically soft and elevated lesions around genitalia or anus.
Human papillomavirus (HPV) is almost always acquired through sexual contact.

answer:
## Bottom line
Genital warts (anogenital warts / condyloma acuminatum) are caused by infection with human papillomavirus (HPV) [1], with low-risk HPV types 6 and 11 responsible for [[F]]about 90% of cases[[/F]] [2][4]; HPV is transmitted primarily through anogenital contact and both penetrative and non-penetrative sexual activity [3].

## Etiology
- HPV is the causative agent of genital warts (as well as cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and cervical cancer, which are caused by different, high-risk HPV types) [1].
- [[F]]HPV types 6 and 11 cause ~90% of genital wart cases[[/F]], consistently reported across sources [2][4][5][8][9][19].
- These low-risk (nononcogenic) HPV types are distinguished from high-risk oncogenic HPV types that drive cervical and other cancers [4][6][13].
- Other HPV types (16, 18, 31, 33, 35) are occasionally found in anogenital warts, usually as co-infections with HPV 6 or 11, and can be associated with high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions, particularly [[K]]in people with HIV infection[[/K]] [7].
- Infection with low-risk HPV 6/11 can also cause benign or low-grade cervical cell abnormalities and respiratory tract papillomas, in addition to anogenital warts [13][17].
- HPV overall comprises over 200 related viruses, with approximately 40 types infecting the anogenital tract [11]; genital warts specifically arise from the low-risk subset of these [6][9].

## Transmission and risk factors
- Transmission is primarily via anogenital contact and both penetrative and non-penetrative sexual activity [3]; HPV is described as the most common sexually transmitted infection [14].
- [[K]]Decreased cell-mediated immunity[[/K]] (e.g., due to pregnancy or HIV infection) is associated with genital warts persisting and spreading more widely [10].

## Clinical presentation
- Low-risk genital HPV infection can produce cauliflower-shaped warts on or around the genitals or anus [17][9].
- Anogenital warts are usually asymptomatic but, depending on size and anatomic location, can be painful or pruritic [18].

## Population
- Findings on HPV-6/11–driven genital warts apply broadly to sexually active individuals with anogenital HPV exposure [1][2][3]; among individuals aged 18–59 years in the US (2013–2016), prevalence was [[F]]1.3% in men and 3.1% in women[[/F]] [12].
- Persons with HIV infection or decreased cell-mediated immunity (including pregnancy) represent a subgroup with increased risk of persistence/spread and of high-grade lesions when co-infected with other HPV types [7][10].
- The high-risk-HPV/cervical-cancer findings [11][20][22][23][24][25][26] describe a distinct disease process (cervical neoplasia/cancer) rather than genital warts themselves, and should not be conflated with the warts etiology.

## Evidence quality
- The core causal claim — HPV, especially types 6 and 11, causes genital warts — is supported by multiple concordant descriptive/reference sources (web-based clinical references, a Merck Manual-type statement, and a clinical-trial background statement) [1][2][4][5][8][9][13][19], indicating consistent characterization across sources rather than a single study.
- [[R]]Trial-registry background statements ([1], [5]) describe study rationale/context, not primary experimental findings on wart causation — the causative role of HPV 6/11 is instead established by the concordant descriptive/epidemiologic statements[[/R]] [2][4][7][8][9][13].
- Prevalence data [12] come from a defined US population survey timeframe (2013–2016), not a causal trial.
- No systematic review, randomized trial, or case-control study directly quantifying HPV-6/11 attribution to genital warts (beyond the "90%" figure) is present in the findings.

## Not addressed
The findings do not cover incubation period, natural history/duration of untreated warts, exact mechanism of HPV entry/viral persistence in keratinocytes, or population-specific incidence trends beyond the single US prevalence estimate cited [12].

question: If I took trazodone when would be the best time to take it?

must_have: Immediate release Trazodone is best taken with or shortly after a meal.
Extended release trazodone is best taken before bedtime on an empty stomach.
Taking immediate release Trazodone with or shortly after a meal can reduce gastrointestinal adverse reactions.
Extended release trazodone might cause drowsiness.
Taking immediate release Trazodone with or shortly after a meal can reduce lightheadedness and postural hypotension.
nice_to_have: Trazodone tablets can be either immediate or extended release.

answer:
## Bottom line
FDA labeling states trazodone [[K]]should be taken shortly after a meal or light snack[[/K]] [1], and because [[F]]drowsiness is a common effect[[/F]] [4], the label advises giving [[F]]"a major portion of the daily dose at bedtime"[[/F]] if drowsiness occurs [2][14]. Dosing is otherwise designed to be given in **divided doses** across the day rather than as a single bedtime dose [3][12].

## Efficacy
- The FDA label frames trazodone as a divided-dose antidepressant regimen: [[F]]starting dose 150 mg/day in divided doses[[/F]], increased by 50 mg/day every 3–4 days [3][7][12], up to 400 mg/day outpatient [8] or 600 mg/day inpatient for more severely depressed patients [9] — this dosing schedule is about *depression* treatment, not sleep timing per se.
- Separately, in a randomized trial in [[K]]Parkinson's disease patients with sleep complaints[[/K]], trazodone (given in an evening/bedtime pattern for sleep) produced a greater decrease in Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) scores than comparators [5][11], and trazodone (alongside clonazepam and melatonin) significantly decreased Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scores [10]. These are sleep-quality/sleepiness *scale* outcomes, not depression-outcome or long-term clinical event data.

## Safety & adverse effects
- Common adverse reactions include drowsiness and dizziness/light-headedness, cited at rates such as [[F]]"Drowsiness 24% 6% 41% 20%"[[/F]] across comparison groups [4] — this is the labeled basis for shifting most of the dose to bedtime [2][14].
- [[F]]Priapism[[/F]] is a rare but serious risk noted in the literature, including a report after a single 100 mg dose, relevant to off-label bedtime/insomnia use [6].
- Tablets should be swallowed whole or split along the score line, not chewed or crushed [13].

## Population
- FDA-labeled indication is [[K]]major depressive disorder (MDD) in adults[[/K]] [15], with dosing designed around divided daily administration [3][7][8][9][12].
- The sleep-timing/ESS/PSQI evidence comes from a trial in [[K]]Parkinson's disease patients with sleep complaints[[/K]] [5][10][11], and off-label insomnia use is described generally in the literature with associated priapism risk [6] — neither directly represents the MDD-labeled population's dosing-timing question.

## Evidence quality
- The meal/bedtime timing and divided-dosing guidance derive from FDA product labeling [1][2][3][7][8][9][12][13][14][15] — authoritative for approved use but not itself a controlled efficacy trial of "best timing."
- The sleep-outcome data [5][10][11] come from a randomized trial in a specific population (Parkinson's disease with sleep complaints), which [[R]]supports a scale-level (ESS/PSQI) finding but does not establish a causal or generalizable "best time to take trazodone" conclusion for the broader population[[/R]].
- The priapism observation [6] is drawn from case-level literature, a lower evidence tier than the labeling or the randomized trial.

## Not addressed
The findings do not include a trial that directly compares different daily timing strategies (e.g., morning vs. divided vs. bedtime-only dosing) for either depression or sleep outcomes in the general population; no head-to-head timing-efficacy or timing-safety trial is reported.

answer:
## Bottom line
Keratosis pilaris (KP) — also called follicular hyperkeratosis or "plucked chicken skin" — is one of the [[K]]most common, benign dermatologic conditions[[/K]], caused by [[F]]keratin accumulation in the hair follicles[[/F]], producing rough, often erythematous or hyperpigmented papules typically on the upper arms, thighs, and buttocks [1][5][14]. It is usually [[K]]asymptomatic[[/K]] and considered a normal variant, though it can cause cosmetic and psychosocial concern and, in some, persist lifelong [1][8][23].

## Efficacy
The findings describe treatment options rather than a single trial's efficacy data:
- **Topical keratolytics** are first-line therapy, followed by topical retinoids and corticosteroids [18][30].
- **Lactic and glycolic acids** were the "preferred topicals," reported to demonstrate efficacy [28].
- **General cutaneous measures** — hydrating skin, avoiding long baths/showers, mild soaps — are recommended alongside topical therapy [18].
- **Ablative lasers**: the CO2 laser "showed efficacy," while erbium:YAG "appeared promising due to fewer adverse effects"; microdermabrasion is an option for treatment-refractory cases [18][29].
- Overall management is described as a "multimodal strategy centred on patient education, topical treatments and laser therapies" [27].

No findings report quantitative outcome measures (e.g., % clearance, response rate, timepoints) for any specific therapy — the evidence gives qualitative efficacy statements only.

## Safety & adverse effects
- KP itself is [[F]]benign and innocuous[[/F]], with diagnosis being clinical and the condition usually asymptomatic, though mild pruritus or cosmetic distress can occur [2][8][25].
- A more severe related group, **keratosis pilaris atrophicans**, involves inflammatory keratotic papules that "may result in alopecia and scarring" — distinguishing it from ordinary KP [17].
- Among lasers, erbium:YAG "appeared promising due to fewer adverse effects" compared with other ablative options, implying a relative (not absolute) safety difference [29]. No other specific adverse effect rates for topical or laser treatments are reported in the findings.

## Population
- Onset is typically in [[K]]early childhood[[/K]], becoming most extensive during the teenage years (second decade of life) [3]; it commonly worsens during puberty [14].
- Prevalence is high: an estimated [[F]]50–80% of adolescents and up to 40% of adults[[/F]] are affected, with onset in early childhood and often diminishing with age [7]. KP affects up to half of normal children and up to three-quarters of children with ichthyosis vulgaris [13].
- Most common sites: upper arms (92%), thighs (59%), and buttocks (30%) [14][7].
- KP is associated with atopic dermatitis, ichthyosis vulgaris, obesity, diabetes mellitus, malnutrition, and syndromes such as Down syndrome and Noonan syndrome [4][10][20].
- Inherited mutations in the **FLG** and **ABCA12** genes have been implicated etiologically, and KP is described as an autosomal dominant disorder [12][13].
- It "may persist throughout a patient's lifetime," making it a concern in adult populations as well as children [23].

## Evidence quality
The cited material consists of narrative/updated reviews and general dermatologic descriptions (europepmc sources) and one reference definition (NCI, via web) [1][11][16] — these are descriptive/observational-level syntheses, not randomized controlled trials or systematic reviews with pooled efficacy data. Treatment claims (e.g., "lactic and glycolic acids... demonstrating efficacy," laser comparisons) come from review-level statements without trial-specific effect sizes, so they should be read as [[R]]expert/review-level summaries rather than quantified RCT evidence[[/R]] [18][28][29][27]. No findings identify a named randomized trial, guideline body, or registry (ClinicalTrials.gov) entry for KP.

## Not addressed
The findings do not provide quantitative efficacy figures (e.g., % improvement, response rates, time to clearance) for any specific treatment, nor comparative trial data head-to-head between therapies, nor detailed adverse-event rates beyond the general "fewer adverse effects" comment for erbium:YAG [18][28][29].

## Bottom line
[[F]]Vaginal (vulvovaginal) yeast infection (VVC) is not classified as a sexually transmitted infection[[/F]]; it results from overgrowth of *Candida* that normally lives in the body, driven by internal factors rather than transmission from a partner [1][4].

## Efficacy
Not applicable — this question concerns transmissibility/etiology, not treatment effectiveness. (Findings [10][11] note that when treatment is needed, antifungal medications are generally effective, but this is not the focus of the question.)

## Safety & adverse effects
Not directly addressed by these findings; no adverse-effect data on transmissibility itself. One antifungal product label warns that during treatment, use of condoms/diaphragms may be compromised and that these devices "may be damaged and fail to prevent pregnancy or sexually transmitted diseases (STDs)" [5] — but this describes a **drug–device interaction risk during use of the product**, not evidence that the yeast infection itself is sexually transmitted [5].

## Population
- [[K]]Applies specifically to vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC)[[/K]], where 10–20% of women asymptomatically harbor *Candida* in the vagina without disease [3].
- Overgrowth is linked to factors such as antibiotic use, hormonal changes (pregnancy, menstrual cycle, birth control), uncontrolled diabetes, and immune status — not to sexual contact [4][9].
- Candida can also be a normal, asymptomatic member of the vaginal and gastrointestinal microbiome [2].
- Candidiasis more broadly can affect other sites (mouth, oesophagus, skin, bloodstream) [8], and yeast infections of the breast/nipple are commonly diagnosed during lactation [6] — these are separate presentations, not evidence of person-to-person sexual spread.
- Most infections are caused by *C. albicans*, with non-albicans species (*C. glabrata*, *C. parapsilosis*, *C. tropicalis*) increasingly implicated in other syndromes (fungemia, UTIs) [7].

## Evidence quality
[[R]]The core claim rests on descriptive/mechanistic web-sourced summaries of candidiasis etiology and a clinical practice-style statement about asymptomatic carriage (10–20% of women)[[/R]], rather than a randomized trial or systematic review of transmission [1][3][4]. Finding [2] explicitly flags that whether recurrence reflects reinfection or persistence of resident yeast is scientifically **unresolved**, which tempers any absolute statement about transmissibility. The product-label finding [5] is regulatory labeling language about device interference during treatment, not epidemiologic transmission evidence.

## Not addressed
The findings do not report controlled studies of partner-to-partner transmission, do not quantify any risk of sexual transmission, and do not address male-partner colonization/treatment data. Whether recurrent VVC in some individuals could involve any reinfection component is explicitly described as unresolved [2], not settled by these findings.
